During the peak of the Trump-China trade war, with tariffs being raised nearly every week, companies like Logitech promptly hiked the prices of their products in the US significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to the manufacturers. However, to date no company has been seen passing refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now attempting to remedy this...

Trump Tariff Fiasco

Last year, Trump seized on the issue of the US trade deficit with China, seemingly believing that imposing higher tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move production back to the US.

That was of course never realistic. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to support mass production of consumer electronics.

Trump has consistently claimed that China pays the tariffs, but in reality these costs are entirely borne by the US brands importing the finished goods, with the additional expense ultimately passed on to consumers through price hikes. At its most extreme, tariff rates reached 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on about half of its product range by as much as 25%.

Consumers Ought to Get Refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that the sums already paid by US businesses must be refunded. That refund process is currently under way.

The issue is that the costs were ultimately met by consumers through higher prices, yet there is no sign that any of the affected companies plan to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has now filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds on behalf of consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac View

The principle here is not in dispute. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to their customers, and are now recouping the money from the government. From a moral standpoint, they ought to return to consumers who bought their products during this period the portion of the purchase price attributable to tariffs.

In practice, however, this is hugely challenging. Logitech would have to identify every relevant transaction across its vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers actually paid, and work out what proportion of that consisted of tariff costs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very intriguing precedent — though it is worth noting that in class actions the only real winners tend to be the lawyers, while the amounts consumers end up receiving are usually very small.
